title: Reporting documents for a cleaning site
moduleTitle: Shared: Job management and service delivery
audience: Supervisors and office staff who set up and run the paperwork for a cleaning site or contract.
learningOutcomes: Sort site documents by purpose: supply, staffing, quality and client reporting
Design a form that records what is needed and nothing more
Set an owner, frequency and retention period for each form in a form register

instruction.heading: Why site documents matter
instruction.body: Site documents create a record that work was requested, done, checked and paid for. The sample proposal lists about a dozen reporting documents, from a material requisition to a daily housekeeping schedule. Each one answers a question a client, an insurer or a supervisor may ask later. Before you add a form, write down the question it answers. If you cannot write the question, the form should not exist.

instruction.heading: Sort the documents by purpose
instruction.body: Group forms by what they prove. Supply forms track what was requested, bought and used: the material requisition, the supply requisition, the stock inventory and the dispenser monitoring sheet. Staffing forms record attendance and overtime: the absence report and the overtime request, plus an endorsement form where a sign-off is needed. Quality forms show the work was checked: the site inspection checklist, the daily restroom checklist and the weekly report. Incident and performance forms form a system of their own and are covered in the next lesson.

instruction.heading: Design a form people will complete
instruction.body: A usable form has a reference number, a date, the site, the name of the person completing it, the item or task, the quantity or result, and a signature or initials. Limit each form to what its question needs. Put the most important field first. Use tick boxes for routine answers and free text only for exceptions. Avoid personal identifiers you do not need. The sample incident and appraisal forms include a personal number field. Do not copy a national identity number field into any form unless a clear legal need has been confirmed.

instruction.heading: Requisitions follow a flow
instruction.body: A material requisition moves through a set flow: the site requests the item, a supervisor approves it, purchasing orders it, the site receives it, and the stock record is updated. Each step needs a named owner and a date. A requisition with no receipt step cannot show what was actually used. The sample requisition has numbered lines, codes, units and quantities, which is a sound basis for this flow.

instruction.heading: Daily and weekly records
instruction.body: A daily checklist should take about a minute to complete, and be complete enough to show that the job was checked. The weekly report summarises the week: hours worked, issues, supplies used, inspection results and open actions. Build the weekly report from the daily records rather than from memory, so that the summary matches what happened on site.

instruction.heading: Control references and versions
instruction.body: The sample uses reference codes made from an operations prefix, a form type and a number. A numbering pattern works only if one person controls it. Keep a form register with the reference, the current version, the owner, the frequency, the place where completed forms are filed and the retention period. Withdraw old versions from the site and date every new version.

instruction.heading: Paper or digital
instruction.body: Paper or digital records both work, as long as each entry can be traced to a person, a date and a site. Where the scope requires photographs, define when they are taken, what they must show and where they are stored, using the photo requirements for your business.

procedure: Write the question each form must answer, and delete any form that has no question.
Group the forms into supply, staffing, quality and client reporting.
Design each form with a reference, date, site, name, item, result and signature.
Remove any personal identifier that the question does not need.
Assign an owner, a frequency and a filing location to each form.
Enter each form in the register with a version number and retention period.
Review completion weekly and follow up missing entries within a set time.

workedExamples.situation: The dispenser monitoring sheet on a site is missing entries on most days. It has eleven columns, and the team says it takes too long to complete.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the supervisor enforce the sheet as it is, or change it?
workedExamples.reasoning: The problem is the design, not the team's discipline. The supervisor reduces the sheet to the four fields the question needs: date, dispenser, stock level and initials. A weekly check by the supervisor confirms completion, and missing entries are followed up the same day. The change is recorded in the register as a new version.

equipmentAndPpe: Clipboard or tablet for site entries

commonErrors.error: Creating forms with no question behind them
commonErrors.prevention: Write the question for each form before designing it.
Name an owner and a review frequency for every form in the register.

commonErrors.error: Collecting personal identifiers that are not needed
commonErrors.prevention: Remove each identifier unless its purpose is written down and confirmed.
Withdraw superseded versions and date each new version.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Forms can hold personal information, including names, contact details and health-related notes. Collect only what is needed, store it securely, and limit access.
Record-keeping and retention periods for workplace. Check with the relevant authority before setting any retention period.

qualityStandard: Every form has a stated question, owner, frequency, reference, version and filing location.
No form collects a personal identifier without a confirmed purpose.
Completion is reviewed weekly, and missing entries are followed up within the set time.
Only current versions are kept on site.
documentationEvidence: Form register with reference, version, owner, frequency and retention period
summary: Each form answers a question, so write the question first.
Group forms by supply, staffing, quality and client reporting.
Design forms for completion, and keep only the fields the question needs.
Control references, versions and retention in one register.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the main purpose of a site record form?
options: To give the client a discount on the next visit
To replace insurance cover for the whole site
To show what was requested, done, checked and paid for
To hide supply costs from the client and the labour

knowledgeChecks.question: A form is rarely completed. What is the best first fix?
options: Add more fields so that people write more and make every field compulsory
Shorten it to the fields the question needs, name an owner, and review completion weekly
Make it an annual form that is filled in once a year by the owner and nobody else
Ask staff to memorise its content and check them on it at the next team meeting

knowledgeChecks.question: Why avoid collecting a national identity number on a routine supply or roster form?
options: Because forms cannot contain numbers and the printer cannot print them
Because the number is the same for every staff member and it is easy to read
Because the number changes each financial year and it is printed on the payslip
Because it is not needed for supply or roster records and adds privacy risk

officialReferences.title: Small business (Office of the Australian Information Commissioner)

officialReferences.covers: Read via summary tool (WebFetch). Says most small businesses with annual turnover of $3 million or less are not covered by the Privacy Act 1988, but some are covered regardless of turnover (for example health service providers and businesses trading in personal information). Does not state records retention periods. Whether the Act applies to a particular business is not settled by this page alone. Publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.
